title: 10 Most Popular Attractions in Ayutthaya 2026 — Wat Mahathat, Wat Chaiwatthanaram, Bang Pa-In Palace — Picked from the Real Thing | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: The 10 most popular attractions in Ayutthaya — Wat Mahathat (Buddha head in banyan roots), Wat Chaiwatthanaram, Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon, Wat Phananchoeng, Wihan Phra Mongkhon Bophit and Wat Phra Si Sanphet, Bang Pa-In Royal Palace, Ayothaya Floating Market, Bueng Phra Ram, and Kong Khong Market — with entry fees, how to get there, parking, and trip-planning tips.

ogTitle: 10 Most Popular Attractions in Ayutthaya 2026 — See Everything in One Day | ThailandAddict
ogDesc: Wat Mahathat, Wat Chaiwatthanaram, Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon, Wat Phananchoeng, Bang Pa-In Royal Palace, Ayothaya Floating Market and more — all in one page with entry fees, directions and tips to make the most of your trip.
intro: Ayutthaya was Thailand's capital for hundreds of years. Today people come to walk among the ancient temples and pagodas scattered across the island city — some are little more than brick ruins on a lawn, others still have towering prangs you can photograph all day. We've gathered the 10 most talked-about spots in one page: from the Buddha head cradled in banyan roots at Wat Mahathat, to the row of prangs at Wat Chaiwatthanaram, all the way to Bang Pa-In Royal Palace and a vintage market. Just over an hour from Bangkok by car or train.
chips: 🛕 Wat Mahathat — Buddha head in banyan roots, the city's defining image
👗 Wear Thai dress for photos beside ancient prangs
🚲 Rent a bike or hop the tram to tour temples on the island
🏯 Bang Pa-In Royal Palace + vintage market

blocks.html:
If you're looking for a city close to Bangkok where you get ancient temples, historic pagodas, and great local food all in one day, Ayutthaya is the answer. The heart of the city is the "island" — surrounded by three rivers — where Wat Mahathat, Wat Phra Si Sanphet, Wihan Phra Mongkhon Bophit, and Bueng Phra Ram all sit within easy reach of each other. Rent a bike or take the tram and you can loop through them comfortably. Cross to the western bank and you'll find Wat Chaiwatthanaram beside the Chao Phraya. Head east and there's Ayothaya Floating Market for a relaxed browse with food and shade. Anyone wanting to go further can drive south to Bang Pa-In, where both the royal palace and Kong Khong vintage market await.

Several spots on this list have become visual shorthand for Ayutthaya recognized around the world. The sandstone Buddha head slowly embraced by banyan roots at Wat Mahathat is the city's most iconic image — every visitor to Ayutthaya stops here for a photo. Wat Chaiwatthanaram has a tall Khmer-style central prang surrounded by symmetrical satellite prangs in a layout that mirrors Mount Meru; on Friday, Saturday and Sunday nights Fine Arts Department opens the grounds with illuminated prangs, turning it into the go-to spot for Thai-dress photography. The massive Chai Mongkhon Pagoda at Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon is the tallest in Ayutthaya — you can climb it for a panoramic view. And Luang Pho To at Wat Phananchoeng is a revered giant Buddha that devotees have come to pray to for centuries. Whether you're planning a day trip or staying overnight, work down this list site by site and you'll come away with temples, history, food, and great photos all in one trip.

blocks.name: Wat Mahathat (Buddha Head in Banyan Roots)
blocks.area: Tha Wasukri, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya District, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya
blocks.signature: The sandstone Buddha head slowly embraced by banyan tree roots — the image the whole world recognizes — plus clusters of ancient prangs and headless Buddha rows you can photograph all day
blocks.priceRange: 10 THB for Thais / 50 THB for foreigners
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Mahathat is one of the first temples that comes to mind when people talk about Ayutthaya. Its heart is the sandstone Buddha head cradled in banyan tree roots — the roots have grown over centuries to embrace it, creating an image the whole world now recognizes. A great fit for history lovers, photography enthusiasts, and international visitors who want to see it in person. The temple sits within the Ayutthaya Historical Park, beside Bueng Phra Ram, and was once the religious center of the Ayutthaya Kingdom, dating back to the reign of King Borommarachathirat I.

The thing you can't miss is the Buddha head in the banyan roots — visitors queue all day to photograph it. The custom here is to kneel or crouch so that your head is lower than the Buddha image out of respect. Beyond that, the surrounding area has a collapsed main prang cluster, ancient chedis, and rows of headless Buddha figures — the whole complex is worth wandering through for photographs. The aesthetic is warm red-orange brick against green lawn; the light is beautiful in the early morning and late afternoon when the sun is lower and the heat is less intense.

Entry is very fair — around 10 THB for Thais and 50 THB for foreigners. If you're planning to visit multiple sites there's a combination ticket available. Open daily, with most Thai sources listing around 08:30–16:30 (some periods extending into the evening — check in advance). Allow 1–2 hours to walk through properly. Google reviews give it 4.7 from over twenty-five thousand reviewers — a genuine reflection of how much people love this place.

Small practical notes: the grounds are large and mostly outdoors, so bring a hat, water, and dress modestly since it's a religious heritage site. Parking is available at the front entrance. Getting here from Bangkok is straightforward — suitable for both solo visitors and day-tour groups. If it's your first time in Ayutthaya, this is where to start.
mustOrder: Buddha head in banyan roots (kneel or crouch lower than the head for the photo)
The collapsed main prang cluster and ancient chedis
Rows of ancient headless Buddha figures around the grounds
Red-brick atmosphere in the slanted morning or evening light
blocks.bestFor: First stop of any Ayutthaya trip — history lovers and photographers, morning or evening

blocks.name: Wat Chaiwatthanaram
blocks.area: Ban Pom, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya District
blocks.signature: Khmer-style central prang surrounded by satellite prangs — beautiful day and night, stunning sunset spot, and Fri–Sat–Sun night illuminations for Thai-dress photography
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Chaiwatthanaram is a heritage site on the west bank of the Chao Phraya River, outside the main island of Ayutthaya. Built in the reign of King Prasat Thong in 1630, its defining feature is the tall Khmer-style central prang standing in the middle of a courtyard, surrounded by satellite prangs and symmetrically arranged chedis that mirror the layout of Mount Meru. You can walk the full circuit of the surrounding gallery. A great fit for history lovers, photography enthusiasts, and anyone wanting to wear Thai dress for period-drama-style photos.

The highlight not to miss is the late afternoon when the setting sun hits the river — the old brick turns gold, and this is widely considered the most beautiful sunset spot in Ayutthaya. Even more special: on Friday, Saturday and Sunday nights, plus public holidays, the Fine Arts Department opens the grounds for evening visits with full illuminations from around 18:00–22:00. Glowing prangs against a dark sky in Thai dress — this is the visual the place is known for.

Entry is very affordable — approximately 10–20 THB for Thais and 50 THB for foreigners. Visitors over 60 enter free. Outside the temple there are rows of Thai-dress rental shops with hair styling and props — rental starts around 200–300 THB with a small add-on for styling. There's a café and parking near the entrance. Daytime opening approximately 08:00–18:30.

Its popularity is real — Google reviews sit at 4.7 from around twenty thousand reviewers. What to know before you go: midday sun is harsh, so bring shade or water. If you're planning the Thai-dress evening session, choose Friday, Saturday or Sunday, and allow time to buy tickets before 21:00 because it gets crowded around sunset.
mustOrder: Khmer central prang surrounded by satellite prangs
Sunset over the Chao Phraya River
Fri–Sat–Sun night illuminations
Thai-dress photos in the period-drama style
blocks.bestFor: Evening and night Thai-dress photos, watching the sunset

blocks.name: Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon
blocks.area: Khlong Suan Phlu, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya District, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya
blocks.signature: The tallest pagoda in Ayutthaya — climb it for a panoramic view, plus a large reclining Buddha to drape with cloth, and rows of yellow-robed Buddha figures arranged beautifully around the base
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon is a landmark that almost every Ayutthaya trip includes. One of the city's oldest temples, originally named Wat Pa Kaeo, its centrepiece is the Chai Mongkhon Pagoda — the tallest in Ayutthaya, measuring roughly 62 meters from base to tip — built as a monument to King Naresuan the Great's victory in single-combat elephant battle. You can climb the stairs to the top for a panoramic view of the surrounding grounds and fields beyond. A great fit for history lovers, temple-goers who want to make merit, and anyone who wants a striking souvenir photograph.

There are several highlights here. The rows of yellow-robed Buddha figures arranged around the base of the pagoda is the temple's signature image — everyone who visits photographs this. The wihan housing the large reclining Buddha (Phra Non) is the other key spot — many people come to drape it with a yellow sash and press coins into the walls as an offering. For those with energy, climbing the pagoda itself is worthwhile: at the top there's a deep shaft where visitors toss coins while making a wish, and the view looking down over the temple grounds is worth the climb. The surrounding gardens and pond offer a shady stroll.

Entry is around 20 THB. There's a large parking lot — easy to drive to. The location is southeast of the main island city in Khlong Suan Phlu subdistrict, not far from the center. Open daily approximately 08:00–17:00. Early morning or late afternoon is more comfortable — the sun is lower and fewer people are around.

This place is genuinely popular — Google score around 4.4 and one of the most-reviewed sites in Thailand. On long weekends and holidays it gets very busy. Dress modestly since it's a royal temple, and bring a hat and umbrella because most of the grounds are outdoors with little shade.
mustOrder: Climb the Chai Mongkhon Pagoda for the panoramic view
Drape yellow cloth over the reclining Buddha
Photograph the rows of yellow-robed Buddhas around the pagoda
Toss a coin in the shaft at the top while making a wish
blocks.bestFor: Temple-goers and history lovers — photography from the pagoda top

blocks.name: Wat Phananchoeng Worawihan
blocks.area: Khlong Suan Phlu, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya District, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya
blocks.signature: Luang Pho To (Phra Phuttha Triratanayak) — a vast revered Buddha figure that people come to pray to for business success and safe travel; long venerated by Thai-Chinese devotees
blocks.priceRange: Free for Thais / 20 THB for foreigners
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Phananchoeng Worawihan is an ancient temple on the banks of the Pa Sak River, opposite the main island city of Ayutthaya. It's one of the most visited temples in the province. The undisputed reason everyone comes is "Luang Pho To" — formally Phra Phuttha Triratanayak — an enormous gilded stucco Buddha figure with a lap width of about 14 meters and a height of nearly 20 meters, filling the wihan so completely you have to crane your neck to take it all in. Said to have been built 26 years before the founding of Ayutthaya, it's a powerful destination for anyone praying for success in trade, work, or safe travel.

This temple has long been sacred to Thai-Chinese devotees, since Luang Pho To is also known as "Sam Po Kong" — making it a continuous stream of Chinese-heritage worshippers. Another highlight is the Shrine of Chao Mae Soi Dok Mak — a beautifully styled Chinese shrine popular with people praying for love, with a poignant legend about a Chinese princess at its heart. Around the temple there are multiple merit-making opportunities: draping cloth over Luang Pho To, pressing gold leaf, and feeding fish at the riverside pier.

The grounds are shaded and peaceful. Reviews consistently describe the temple as well-maintained and clean, with both covered and open parking for a large number of vehicles. Free entry for Thais; 20 THB for foreigners. Open daily approximately 08:00–17:00. It's a short walk over a bridge from the main town — allow 1–2 hours to visit comfortably.

Worth knowing: on long weekends and festivals — especially Chinese New Year and the Thai New Year — this place gets extremely busy. If crowds aren't your thing, arriving early in the morning is the smarter call. Some bathroom facilities are a fair walk from the parking area, so allow time for that. Overall, a stop in Ayutthaya that genuinely deserves its place on the list.
mustOrder: Pray before Luang Pho To (Phra Phuttha Triratanayak) in the wihan
Pray for love at the Shrine of Chao Mae Soi Dok Mak
Drape cloth over Luang Pho To
Feed fish at the Pa Sak riverside pier
blocks.bestFor: Merit-making and praying for business success or safe travel — go early morning to avoid the crowds
blocks.zone: Pa Sak riverside — opposite island city

blocks.name: Wihan Phra Mongkhon Bophit and Wat Phra Si Sanphet
blocks.area: Island city, Pratu Chai, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya District, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya
blocks.signature: The wihan houses Phra Mongkhon Bophit — a large, reverent bronze Buddha in deep black. Next door is Wat Phra Si Sanphet with its three Lankan-style chedis in a row, the most reproduced image of old Ayutthaya.
blocks.descHtml:
When people think of Ayutthaya's visual identity, many see three bell-shaped chedis in a line. Those are at Wat Phra Si Sanphet, the former royal temple inside the ancient palace grounds. Just to the south and nearly adjacent is Wihan Phra Mongkhon Bophit, which enshrines Phra Mongkhon Bophit — a large bronze Buddha in deep lustrous black, with a serene expression. These two sites share a boundary and are close enough to walk between, making them a near-universal stop for everyone visiting Ayutthaya. A great fit for anyone wanting to photograph the ancient capital's most iconic architecture, as well as devotees who come to pray.

The highlight not to miss is the three Lankan-style chedis at Wat Phra Si Sanphet, built to hold the ashes of Ayutthaya's kings. Most reviews agree that the best photo angle is standing so all three chedis line up perfectly — this is the defining image of Ayutthaya. In Wihan Phra Mongkhon Bophit, many visitors are struck by the sheer scale of the bronze figure — you have to look upward to see the full face. The wihan interior is cool and calm, with a steady stream of worshippers. Outside there are souvenir stalls and a food area to walk around.

Entry is very reasonable — Wihan Phra Mongkhon Bophit is free; Wat Phra Si Sanphet is around 10 THB for Thais and 50 THB for foreigners. The location is in the middle of the island city in Pratu Chai subdistrict, within the historical park — easy to get to with convenient parking. The wihan opens approximately 08:00 into the evening; the temple approximately 08:30–16:30. Morning and late afternoon offer better light and less heat, since the grounds are mostly open with little shade.

This is popular because it genuinely is the heart of old Ayutthaya — you get historic grandeur, beautiful architecture, and a place to pray all together. Consistent high Google scores. Dress modestly since it's a sacred site, bring a hat and water, and allow a little extra time if you want to explore additional heritage sites nearby in the park.
mustOrder: Three Lankan-style chedis at Wat Phra Si Sanphet
Phra Mongkhon Bophit — large bronze Buddha in the wihan
The three-chedis-in-a-row photo angle
blocks.bestFor: Photographing the ancient capital's most iconic architecture — morning or afternoon

blocks.title: 🛏️ Find a place to stay in Ayutthaya
blocks.text: If you're planning to spend more than a day in Ayutthaya, staying on the island puts Wat Mahathat, Wat Phra Si Sanphet, and Bueng Phra Ram within easy walking or cycling distance — ideal for catching sites before the crowds arrive. If you prefer a relaxed atmosphere, riverfront stays and traditional Thai-house guesthouses are scattered all around the city. Arriving early at the temples is easier when you're already nearby. Compare prices across multiple sites before booking — during high season at year-end and on long weekends, well-located rooms fill fast.

blocks.name: Bang Pa-In Royal Palace
blocks.area: Bang Pa-In District, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya
blocks.signature: Multiple buildings in Thai, Chinese and European styles spread across gardens and wide ponds — Phra Thinang Aisawan Tiphya-At, the golden Thai-style pavilion in the middle of the water, is the photo everyone takes
blocks.descHtml:
Bang Pa-In Royal Palace is an historic summer residence on the Chao Phraya River in Bang Pa-In District, south of the Ayutthaya island city — about 60 km from Bangkok. What makes people fall for this place is the mix of architectural styles in one location: Thai, Chinese and European buildings spread across wide gardens and large ponds. If it's your first visit, Phra Thinang Aisawan Tiphya-At — a golden Thai-style four-sided pavilion standing in the middle of the water — is the picture everyone leaves with. A great fit for history lovers, photography enthusiasts, families with children, and anyone wanting to show foreign visitors a genuine expression of Thai beauty.

Beyond the water pavilion, highlights include Phra Thinang Wehat Chamrun — a striking red Chinese-style pavilion — Ho Withun Thasana, a tall colorful observatory tower you can climb for a full-palace view, and Phra Thinang Warophat Phiman. Across the river there's Wat Niwet Thammaprawat, built in a Gothic-Christian style completely unlike any Thai temple — a genuine surprise. The palace grounds cover over 160 rai, beautifully landscaped with large trees and a breeze running through. Most reviews praise the cleanliness, the quality of maintenance at every corner, and the relaxed pace of walking through all day.

Entry is excellent value: 30 THB for Thai adults, 20 THB for students, 100 THB for foreigners. Golf cart rental is available at around 400 THB/hour if you'd rather not walk. Open daily 08:00–17:00 but tickets stop selling around 15:30 — allow at least half a day. Getting here from Bangkok is easy whether you drive, take the train, or stop on the way to Ayutthaya. Google score 4.4 from over five thousand reviews — visitors genuinely enjoy it. Tips before you go: this is a royal precinct, so dress modestly — no spaghetti straps, crop tops, or very short shorts or skirts. Cover-up cloths are available at the entrance for a small fee. Some buildings can't be entered or photographed — watch the signs at each spot. Morning or late afternoon gives better light and less heat for the outdoors walks. Bring a hat and water.
mustOrder: Phra Thinang Aisawan Tiphya-At — golden Thai pavilion in the water
Phra Thinang Wehat Chamrun — red Chinese-style pavilion
Ho Withun Thasana — observation tower with palace views
Wat Niwet Thammaprawat — Gothic-style temple across the river
blocks.bestFor: History lovers and photography — a half-day trip close to Bangkok

blocks.name: Ayothaya Floating Market
blocks.area: Phai Ling, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya District, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya
blocks.cuisine: Thai food / Traditional Thai sweets / Street food
blocks.signature: Ayutthaya's largest retro floating market across 80 rai of traditional Thai houses — vendors in Thai dress paddling boats, sweet and savory food, OTOP souvenirs, boat rides, and Thai performance shows
blocks.descHtml:
Ayothaya Floating Market is the largest retro floating market in Ayutthaya — 80 rai of traditional Thai riverside houses with vendors in Thai dress paddling boats of goods, creating an atmosphere that feels like stepping back into the old kingdom. A great fit for families, photography enthusiasts, and anyone wanting one place that combines eating, sightseeing, and photo opportunities. Multiple reviewers say it "feels like you've traveled back to the Ayutthaya period." If it's your first visit to Ayutthaya and you want one place that covers food, scenery, and photography, this fits the brief.

The highlights not to miss include the boat ride around the market, the Ayutthaya historical performance and Thai dance shows on stage (multiple sessions on Saturdays and Sundays), Thai-dress rental for retro photos, and the food zone with a wide range of sweet and savory items. Real reviews specifically mention rare traditional Thai sweets made fresh — small rice-flour cups, traditional confections hard to find in the capital. There are also OTOP souvenirs, handicrafts, and an elephant ride zone. A comfortable 1–3 hour browse.

Free entry for Thais, budget for food is gentle and prices are low. Foreign visitors pay around 200 THB for the performance show. Open daily 09:00–18:00. Located in Phai Ling subdistrict, east of the island city, near Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon — under 2 hours from Bangkok. Parking is available.

Worth knowing: weekends are far busier and livelier — shows run multiple sessions and the place hums with activity. On weekdays it's quieter and some stalls may be closed. If you want the full experience, come on a weekend. Watch your step on the riverside walkways and do a first lap around the market before you start buying.
mustOrder: Boat ride around the market
Ayutthaya historical performance / Thai dance show
Traditional Thai sweets made fresh
Thai-dress rental for retro photos
blocks.zone: Phai Ling (eastern side of island city)

blocks.name: Bueng Phra Ram Public Park
blocks.area: Island city, Pratu Chai, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya District, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya
blocks.signature: A large pond at the heart of the old city, turned into a shaded public park — free to enter, great for a stroll, cycling, feeding fish, and sitting by the water, with beautiful sunset views over an ancient prang backdrop in the evening
blocks.descHtml:
Bueng Phra Ram is a wide natural pond at the center of the Ayutthaya island city, turned into a shaded public park with free entry. It sits right beside Wat Mahathat and the heritage site cluster — making it a natural rest stop after walking temples all day. If you want a quiet waterside seat, a stroll under shady trees, or a change of pace from pure heritage-site touring, this spot is ideal. Most reviews describe it simply as "quiet and peaceful," and people mention loving the large trees providing shade throughout the day.

The highlight most people talk about is the evening, when the sun sets behind the old prangs — the light turns everything warm and several people come here specifically to photograph this. Beyond sitting and watching, you can also stroll, cycle around the pond, and feed fish. There's a small island in the middle with a Buddha figure and a pavilion to visit. A frequently noted detail in reviews is the monitor lizards that regularly wander along the waterside — a touch of old-city character, best admired from a distance.

Entry is free, parking for bikes and motorbikes is easy around the pond. The location is right in the middle of the island city next to Wat Mahathat — from here you can walk or cycle to other sites with no effort. An outdoor park open all day, but the best times are early morning when the air is cool and the hour before sunset. Google score 4.4 from nearly two thousand reviews — locals and visitors both make use of it.

Worth knowing: some walkways include bridges and uneven ground — not ideal for wheelchair users or the elderly. The midday sun can still be intense even with tree cover, so bring water and a hat. And pack out your rubbish — this is a historic site precinct.
mustOrder: Sunset over the ancient prang backdrop
Stroll or cycle around the pond
Feed fish at the water's edge
Visit the Buddha figure on the island in the middle
blocks.bestFor: Relaxing waterside break after temple-touring — sunset views over ancient prangs

blocks.name: Wat Ratchaburana
blocks.area: Tha Wasukri, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya District, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya
blocks.signature: Descend a narrow steep staircase into the crypt beneath the main prang — nearly 600-year-old murals inside, and the chamber where vast treasures of gold and Buddha images from Ayutthaya were discovered
blocks.priceRange: 10 THB for Thais / 50 THB for foreigners
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Ratchaburana is one of the most beautiful and story-rich temples on the Ayutthaya island. Built in 1424 during the reign of King Borommarachathirat II (Chao Sam Phraya) as a memorial to two princes who died fighting each other on elephant-back for the throne, its large Khmer-style prang rises prominently from the grounds. A great fit for history enthusiasts who love photographing ancient architecture, or anyone wanting a quiet, atmospheric wander. It sits directly beside Wat Mahathat — cross the road and you're there, easy to visit both in one sweep.

The highlight not to miss is the "crypt" beneath the main prang — you descend a narrow, steep staircase into the chamber below. Inside there are ancient murals nearly 600 years old to view up close, and this is the chamber where an enormous cache of gold objects and Buddha images from the Ayutthaya period were once discovered. The real artifacts are now displayed at the Chao Sam Phraya National Museum — if you want to see the actual gold, that's the follow-up stop. For photographers, try arriving late afternoon when the soft angled light hits the prang walls beautifully.

Entry is very affordable — 10 THB for Thais, 50 THB for foreigners. Open daily 08:00–18:00 (some periods have evening lighting sessions — check before going). A trip through Ayutthaya barely costs much in entry fees at all — whatever you save is better spent on a bike rental or tram to loop the island. The temple sits in the middle of the island city, near Bueng Phra Ram, Wat Mahathat, and Wihan Phra Mongkhon Bophit — all walkable or cycleable from here.

People talk about this place because beyond the beautiful and well-preserved prang, the experience of descending into the crypt to see the murals up close is genuinely rare — a real physical closeness to history. A small tip: wear shoes you can move in, since the crypt stairs are steep and some surfaces are slippery. Bring water and a hat since the temple grounds are mostly open. Come in the morning or late afternoon for cooler conditions. Dress modestly — this is an important World Heritage registered site.
mustOrder: Descend into the crypt to see ancient murals
The main Khmer-style prang
Follow up at Chao Sam Phraya National Museum to see the real gold treasures

blocks.name: Kong Khong Market (Baan Saeng Som)
blocks.area: Bang Pa-In District, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya
blocks.signature: Retro market in a cluster of old Thai wooden houses — browse traditional Thai sweets, affordable local food, antiques, home décor and vintage kitchenware in a cool shaded setting
blocks.descHtml:
If you want to feel the atmosphere of old Ayutthaya in a tangible way, Kong Khong Market (Baan Saeng Som) is the place to walk through. A retro market set in a cluster of old Thai wooden houses, vendors in pink-purple Thai dress lay their wares low on the ground so buyers have to stoop to browse — which is the origin of the name "Kong Khong" (stooping and bending). Great for a relaxed browse and some food, a family outing, or visiting with older relatives. It's close to Bang Pa-In Royal Palace right on the highway from Bangkok, so it's very easy to stop by.

The things reviewers mention most are the traditional Thai sweets — kanom thuay ta lai, rich and creamy with a faint sweetness, sold in sets of 3 for 10 THB — as well as roti sai mai, thua tat, and rare old-fashioned sweets that are hard to find in Bangkok anymore. Local food starts from the tens of baht. The other enjoyable corner is the antiques and home décor zone: basketware, pottery, vintage plates and bowls, and old-school kitchenware to browse at leisure — collectors will find this particularly satisfying.

The atmosphere is pleasant — there's a roof overhead so you're not walking in direct sun, and the whole market is kept clean and tidy. Two seating areas are available for eating. Reviews say it feels shaded and cool to walk through, though midday can still get warm as with any outdoor market. Free entry, free parking, and a few hundred baht per person covers food and something to take home.

Worth knowing: open only Thursday–Sunday and on public holidays, approximately 09:00–16:00. Come in the morning through early afternoon as stalls begin closing later in the day. The draw is real Thai retro atmosphere, genuinely good cheap food, and an easy stop on the road into Ayutthaya — which is why it's been a reliable visitor favorite for years.
mustOrder: Kanom thuay ta lai (3 cups for 10 THB)
Roti sai mai
Thua tat and traditional Thai sweets
Antiques, home décor and vintage kitchenware zone
blocks.bestFor: Morning family browse for traditional Thai sweets — weekends

blocks.title: What to know before you visit Ayutthaya

items.title: Getting around the city
items.text: On the main island, renting a bicycle or motorbike is popular, and there are heritage trams that loop between temples. Temples outside the island — like Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon and Bang Pa-In — are further out, so a Grab or rented vehicle is more flexible. Public transport is limited.

items.title: Carry cash
items.text: Heritage site entry fees, retro markets, and street food stalls mostly take cash. Bring small bills and coins — it's much more convenient than waiting to pay by app, especially at market stalls and vintage-market vendors.

items.title: Beat the sun and the queues
items.text: Ayutthaya is hot almost all year round. Start temple visits before 10am or in the late afternoon for the most comfortable conditions. Wat Chaiwatthanaram in the evening and on Fri–Sat–Sun nights draws big crowds — allow extra time to find parking.

items.title: Dress for temples
items.text: Temples are sacred sites — dress modestly with covered shoulders and knees. If you want to wear Thai dress for photos, there are rental shops with hair and makeup all around the island city and near Wat Chaiwatthanaram.

items.title: Language and signage
items.text: Main tourist sites and ticket booths usually have English signage. Markets and local shops may have limited English — a translation app or pointing at photos helps a lot.

items.title: Prepare for the walk
items.text: Bring water, a hat, and sun protection — many heritage sites are open grounds with little shade. Wear shoes you can remove easily, since some wihans and chapels require shoes off before entering.

blocks.title: Planning an efficient one-day Ayutthaya trip
blocks.html:
The most comfortable approach to Ayutthaya is to divide it by zone. Start the morning on the island before the sun gets strong — work through Wat Mahathat, Wat Phra Si Sanphet, and Wihan Phra Mongkhon Bophit, which are all within walking distance of each other, then rest at Bueng Phra Ram nearby. At midday, eat and escape the heat at Ayothaya Floating Market. In the late afternoon, head to Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon and Wat Phananchoeng on the Khlong Suan Phlu side. Finish at Wat Chaiwatthanaram for the sunset — if you're there on a Friday, Saturday or Sunday, wait a little longer for the night illuminations (approximately 18:00–21:00) to get that glowing prangs-in-Thai-dress shot. If you have a full free day, drive down to Bang Pa-In afterward for the royal palace and Kong Khong Market.

On entry fees: for most major heritage sites, Thais pay around 10 THB and foreigners pay 50 THB (Wat Mahathat, Wat Ratchaburana, Wat Phra Si Sanphet, Wat Chaiwatthanaram). Wihan Phra Mongkhon Bophit and Bueng Phra Ram are free. Wat Phananchoeng is free for Thais and 20 THB for foreigners. Bang Pa-In Royal Palace is 30 THB for Thais and 100 THB for foreigners. Bring cash — small bills and coins — since many sites collect entry fees in cash. Ayutthaya is hot nearly year-round, so pack a hat, umbrella and water. Temples are sacred places — dress modestly with covered shoulders and knees.

blocks.text: If you're planning to spend more than a day in Ayutthaya at a relaxed pace, staying on the island or by the river puts you close to the temples — rise early to catch the heritage sites before the crowds arrive. Compare prices across multiple sites before you book, since well-located rooms fill fast during high season at year-end and on long weekends.

faq.a: The ones nearly everyone visiting Ayutthaya stops at are Wat Mahathat, where the Buddha head is cradled in banyan roots — the city's most iconic image — followed by Wat Chaiwatthanaram with its row of prangs by the river, Wat Phra Si Sanphet and its three Lankan-style chedis, Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon with the tallest pagoda in Ayutthaya, and Wat Phananchoeng with the giant Luang Pho To. If time allows, add Bang Pa-In Royal Palace.

faq.q: What makes Ayutthaya special — why do people visit?
faq.a: Ayutthaya was Thailand's capital for hundreds of years. Its appeal is the concentration of ancient temples and pagodas spread across the island city — you can walk or cycle between them all day. The most universally recognized image is the Buddha head in banyan roots at Wat Mahathat. Wat Chaiwatthanaram offers night illuminations every Friday, Saturday and Sunday, making it the most popular Thai-dress photography spot in the country. Beyond temples there's Bang Pa-In Royal Palace blending Thai, Chinese and European architecture, and retro markets to browse.

faq.q: How much does entry cost at each Ayutthaya attraction?
faq.a: Most major heritage sites charge Thais around 10 THB and foreigners 50 THB — including Wat Mahathat, Wat Ratchaburana, Wat Phra Si Sanphet, and Wat Chaiwatthanaram. Wihan Phra Mongkhon Bophit and Bueng Phra Ram are free. Wat Phananchoeng is free for Thais and 20 THB for foreigners. Bang Pa-In Royal Palace is 30 THB for Thais and 100 THB for foreigners. Bring cash for entry fees.

faq.q: How do I get to Ayutthaya, and is parking easy?
faq.a: Ayutthaya is about an hour and a half from Bangkok — drive via the Asia Highway or take a train or minivan into the city. On the island, the popular choices are bicycle rental, motorbike rental, or the heritage tram that loops the temples. If you drive yourself, the main temples and Bang Pa-In Royal Palace all have car parks. For a day covering multiple sites, having your own wheels or a rental is more flexible, since some temples are outside the island.

faq.q: What are the opening hours? Does Wat Chaiwatthanaram really open at night?
faq.a: Most heritage sites open during the day around 08:00–18:00. Bueng Phra Ram is accessible all day as an outdoor park. Ayothaya Floating Market is open daily approximately 09:00–18:00. Wat Chaiwatthanaram does open for night visits with full illuminations — but only on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays, approximately 18:00–21:00. This is the period people dress in Thai costume for the evening photographs. Check the latest hours before you go, since they may vary by season and festival.
